PullRequest.Title: chat: register Agents Window settings in editor
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

- register the unified workspace picker and merged-session cleanup settings from the shared workbench chat contribution
- reuse the shared setting identifiers from the Agents Window contributions
- add regression coverage that verifies the normal workbench contribution registers all three settings

This fixes the settings added by #334341 and #334554 appearing as unknown in the normal `settings.json` editor.

## Validation

- `git diff --check`
- repository commit hooks
- compile, targeted tests, and hygiene were not run locally because dependency restoration was blocked by the sandbox from writing `/Users/meganrogge/Library/Caches/ms-playwright`

Scenarios.Scenario: Cold startup of the normal VS Code workbench and opening/searching Settings for Agents Window options
Scenarios.CriticalPath: ES module evaluation of chat.shared.contribution synchronously imports agentSessionsConfiguration, localizes three descriptions, allocates one three-property schema object, and registers it before startup continues. No subprocess, filesystem, database, network, or IPC must complete for registration.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Exactly three configuration properties, once per renderer module lifetime; cost does not scale with sessions, repositories, settings-file size, or UI events.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Serialized ES module evaluation; module caching guarantees one evaluation and one registration per renderer context.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Cold startup evaluates the module once. Warm accesses to Settings reuse the configuration registry; there is no repeated registration, cache key, negative cache, or miss-driven work.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence: the added static import and registration body are fully traced, and they contain only synchronous in-process object/registry work.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact startup micro-cost is unmeasured, but the work is constant-size and the imported nls, product, agentHostSchema, registry, and chat constants dependencies are already imported by the parent shared contribution.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The diff intentionally makes three settings available in the normal workbench with bounded one-time work and no expensive boundary.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agents Window startup and use of unified workspace picker / merged-session lifecycle settings
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The same shared contribution registers all three settings during module initialization. Runtime picker and cleanup consumers only read the unchanged string keys; this diff does not add work to picker rendering, session enumeration, GitHub polling, archival, or deletion paths.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Mirror registered agent-host configuration values in a RootConfigChanged patch when an Agent Host connects/reconnects or a relevant global setting changes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One existing patch per host connect/reconnect; at most one patch per explicit user change to either cleanup setting while connected. Both values are scalar integers and are coalesced into the existing connect patch.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: In the Agents Window these same cleanup schemas and agentHost mappings were already registered by github.contribution, so connect/change IPC behavior and call count were already present; the diff relocates registration without increasing boundary cardinality.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The connect patch is part of an existing Agent Host initialization path; this diff does not start the host or add an extra connect-time IPC. A user setting edit can add one small patch, off startup and picker critical paths.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Registration remains three properties once per Agents Window renderer. Subsequent configuration reads are unchanged and do not scale differently with workspace or session count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One serialized module registration. Existing session/GitHub contribution consumers retain their prior scheduling; no new loops, queues, or concurrency are introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: ES module caching coalesces the shared registration. Before the diff, the unified-picker setting and the two cleanup settings were registered by two sessions-specific modules; after the diff they are registered together by one shared module, so there is no duplicate warm-path work.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence: all changed consumers preserve identical setting strings, and the old registration blocks are removed as the shared registration is added.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: No material uncertainty in multiplicity; exact registry and IPC serialization timings are unmeasured but payload and call count are tightly bounded.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Registration is consolidated, and the product workflows retain the same runtime consumers and expensive-boundary cardinality.

Scenarios.Scenario: Normal-workbench Agent Host connection and edits to merged-session cleanup settings
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Registration adds two agentHost metadata entries. It does not create or connect an Agent Host. If a host is already connecting, resolving all mirrored settings and dispatching its existing root-config patch is on that connection path; explicit edits are user-triggered and dispatch after the configuration event.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the existing RootConfigChanged action containing renderer-owned configuration to an already-created Agent Host.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One IPC on each existing connect/reconnect, with two extra scalar fields after this diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The connect/reconnect path already dispatched one complete root-config patch. In the normal workbench these two fields were absent because their schemas were not registered there.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: No additional IPC round trip is added; only the payload of the existing initialization message grows by two integer properties.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send a root-config patch after an explicit global edit to either newly recognized cleanup setting.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one IPC per relevant user edit while a host is connected; one scalar field is sent.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: These settings were not registered in the normal workbench, so they were not entries in the declarative agent-host sync map and such an edit did not dispatch this setting-specific patch.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The patch follows a rare explicit settings change and is not on startup, rendering, scrolling, or input-frame critical paths.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Two additional integer lookups and two scalar patch fields per connect/reconnect. A relevant edit affects one setting and produces one patch; cost is independent of session and repository count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Existing protocol-client sequencing sends the single root-config action; the diff adds no Promise fan-out, concurrent host launches, or unbounded queue.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Registry metadata is retained for the renderer lifetime as intended. Connect/reconnect rebuilds the existing full patch; there is no new cache, miss behavior, or retained per-session state.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence: registry insertion and both IPC call sites are directly traced; the metadata consumer never instantiates a host.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The frequency of users changing cleanup settings or reconnecting hosts is unknown, but each occurrence is one bounded scalar patch rather than collection-scaled work.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. The only new boundary behavior is one small IPC after a deliberate setting change; connect-time IPC count is unchanged and payload growth is constant.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all nine changed files and every diff hunk. Traced cold/warm module registration, shared versus Agents Window startup, configuration-registry processing, transitive Agent Host IPC, effective cardinality, concurrency, and cache/lifecycle behavior. No high-confidence actionable performance regression was introduced, and the PR is not evidenced as a performance-regression fix.
